opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so feedback is really central to how we think about scouts. A scout is something you set up to keep an eye on the web for you, something you care about over time. When it sends you a report, there's a lot of signal in how you react to it.

At the simplest level, it's explicit feedback. You might say "this was useful," or "I don't care about this kind of update," or "only tell me when the price actually drops below this threshold." The scout should take that in and adjust what it looks for, how it filters, and how it presents things next time. You shouldn't have to go back and rewrite your original instructions. Ideally you just react naturally, the way you would with a human assistant, and it gets better.

What I find more interesting is that people often don't know exactly what they want when they first set up a scout. They have a rough intent, like "keep me posted on new restaurants opening in my neighborhood." Only when they see a few reports do they realize, "Actually, I don't care about chains," or "I really want to know when reservations open." So feedback isn't just correcting mistakes. It's helping the user and the agent figure out the real intent together over time.

Then there's the presentation side. Some people want a one-line summary with a link. Others want more context, or comparisons with what changed since last time. Learning those preferences makes the reports feel less like a generic alert and more like something written for you.

The hard part is generalizing the right amount. If someone says "not this one," you want to understand why, so you don't overcorrect and stop sending things they actually would have wanted. Sometimes that means the scout should ask a clarifying question rather than guess.

Long term, the vision is that a scout gets noticeably better the longer you use it. It's not a static query running on a schedule. It's an agent that's learning what matters to you, so over time you trust it more and you have to think about it less.

r001.rationale: The response says feedback should change what the scout looks for, filters, and presents next time, but does not clearly state that feedback is incorporated into the agent’s instructions for its next run.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that a scout is essentially doing research on your behalf, and the quality of that research depends a lot on how well it understands what you actually care about. When you first set one up, you give it a prompt — "keep me updated on advances in multimodal reasoning" or whatever it is — and that prompt is necessarily underspecified. You don't know yet what you'll find interesting, and the scout certainly doesn't.

So the feedback loop is where the real value comes from. Every time you react to a report — you say "this part was great, go deeper here," or "I don't care about this product launch stuff, I care about the technical results," or even just which items you click on and which you skip — that's signal about your preferences that was never captured in the original prompt. And the scout can fold that back in, so the next report is more tailored, more relevant, and spends its effort on the things you actually want.

What I find compelling is that this is much closer to how you'd work with a human research assistant. You wouldn't hand them a one-line brief and expect perfection forever. You'd give them notes after the first few drafts, and they'd calibrate. The difference is that with an AI scout, that calibration can happen continuously and at scale — it can keep learning across many reports, and it never gets tired of being told to adjust.

And there's a longer-term angle too. If you think about where this goes, the feedback isn't just adjusting the content of a single scout's reports. It's building up a richer model of you — your taste, your expertise level, what you already know and don't need repeated. That model can transfer to other tasks, so the system as a whole gets better at serving you, not just that one scout. That's the thing I'm most excited about.

r001.rationale: The response says feedback is folded back in to tailor the next report, but it does not state that the feedback is incorporated into the scout’s instructions for its next run.

astra-6.text:
I think user feedback can help a scout learn what makes a report useful to that particular person. Did it surface something new? Was it relevant? Was there enough detail to understand why it mattered? If a user says, “I already knew this,” or “This is interesting, but I’d like you to go deeper,” that gives the scout a signal about what to look for and how to present it next time.

The important thing is that the feedback carries forward. It shouldn’t just improve the report you’re looking at; it should inform future reports. And you want to balance that personalization with discovery, so the scout still brings you things you wouldn’t have thought to ask for.

r001.rationale: The response says feedback can guide what the scout looks for and how it presents future reports, but does not state that feedback is incorporated into the agent’s instructions for its next run.

sol-6.1.text: I think of it as a feedback loop. If a user tells the scout, “This was useful,” or “You missed something important,” that gives it a signal about what to look for and emphasize next time. And that feedback can be about the substance—what information matters—or the presentation, like how much detail the user wants. Over time, the reports should become more aligned with that user’s needs, without the user having to repeat all of those preferences every time.

r001.rationale: The response says feedback guides what the scout looks for and emphasizes in future reports, but does not state that it is incorporated into the scout agent’s instructions for its next run.
